observation_summary: The StopWatch class incorrectly updates the stopTime when stop() is called even if the watch is already in a suspended state, causing the total time to increase erroneously.
hypothesis: The stop() method lacks a conditional check to ensure that the stopTime is only updated if the watch is currently in the RUNNING state. If the watch is already SUSPENDED, the stopTime should not be overwritten by the current system time.
prediction: The fix will involve wrapping the stopTime assignment in an if-statement that checks if the current state is STATE_RUNNING.
experiment_rationale: The provided fix diff shows exactly this: an if-condition (if(this.runningState == STATE_RUNNING)) was added around the stopTime assignment, confirming that the missing check was the root cause.
reasoning_summary: The bug is caused by a missing validation check (a guard) in the stop() method. The method was unconditionally updating the stopTime, which is incorrect when the watch is already suspended. Adding the missing state check correctly prevents the time from being updated when it shouldn't be. This fits the definition of a 'Checking' defect.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the logic is procedural, the root cause is specifically the absence of a guard condition to validate the state before performing an operation, which is the hallmark of a Checking defect.
